title: India's Got Latent Almost Destroyed Two Careers — Now Everyone Is Defending Samay Raina and Ranveer Allahbadia
excerpt: RJ Mahvash is the latest voice backing the controversial duo. The legal fight isn't over, but the cultural tide has turned.
body:
Samay Raina broke Indian YouTube. Then Indian YouTube almost broke him. Now he's back — and the people who once called for his head are lining up to defend him.

RJ Mahvash, one of the more prominent voices in India's radio and digital entertainment scene, went public this week in support of both Raina and Ranveer Allahbadia — the two creators at the centre of the *India's Got Latent* firestorm that consumed the first half of 2026. "Humans do mistakes," Mahvash said in an interview with Pinkvilla. "I will still support them."

It's a statement that would have been career suicide three months ago. The fact that it's now a defensible position tells you how much the conversation has shifted.

## The Controversy, Recapped

For diaspora audiences who may have caught only the headlines: *India's Got Latent* was Samay Raina's YouTube comedy show that became one of the most-watched Indian digital series of 2025. The trouble started when guest judge Ranveer Allahbadia made remarks about parents that crossed every line imaginable. The clip went viral for all the wrong reasons.

What followed was a cascade: FIRs filed across multiple states, over 40 individuals summoned by the Maharashtra Cyber Cell, the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting ordering action, and — in a move that stunned the creator economy — the Supreme Court stepping in. Allahbadia received interim protection but had his passport seized. Raina pulled every *India's Got Latent* video from YouTube.

For months, two of India's biggest digital creators went dark.

## The Comeback Trail

The tide has been turning since April. Raina and Allahbadia appeared together on *The Great Indian Kapil Show*, where Kapil Sharma — who had privately warned Raina before the controversy hit — roasted both of them about the saga. The audience laughed. India moved on, at least partly.

Raina posted his first members-only YouTube video in late April, garnering nearly 8,000 likes within an hour. A leaked date for *India's Got Latent Season 2* — May 9, 2026 — circulated widely, attributed to producer Balraj Ghai. Though no official confirmation has come, Raina himself has acknowledged that Season 2 is in development, with a format adjusted to avoid future legal minefields.

Bharti Singh has defended Raina publicly. So has Mahvash. The narrative is shifting from "cancel them" to "let them learn and come back."

## Why NRIs Care

Here's the thing about *India's Got Latent*: its audience was never just in India. Young Indians in the US, UK, Canada, and Australia were among the show's most engaged viewers. Indian-origin students in dorms from Ann Arbor to Melbourne watched Raina's roasts the way a previous generation watched *Comedy Circus*.

The legal saga — passport seizures, Supreme Court hearings, cyber cell summons — played out in real time on social media that doesn't respect borders. For diaspora viewers, it raised uncomfortable questions about the boundaries of digital comedy in India, the growing power of online outrage to trigger criminal proceedings, and whether creators can survive a cancellation cycle.

Mahvash's defence isn't just about two individuals. It's about whether India's digital entertainment ecosystem has room for second chances — something the diaspora, living in cultures with their own complex histories of cancellation and redemption, is watching with particular interest.

## What's Next

The legal proceedings aren't over. Allahbadia's passport remains with the court. The FIRs haven't been quashed. But the cultural momentum has clearly shifted toward rehabilitation.

If Season 2 happens — and everything suggests it will — it won't just be a comedy show. It'll be a test case for whether India's creator economy can mature past its first major cancellation crisis.
